tokyo3_y_28.gf_detail: Real, purpose-built GF items exist: a グルテンフリー塩ラーメン (gluten-free SHIO/salt ramen) using brown-rice noodles from Shimane, developed by the founder specifically with wheat-allergy and celiac diners in mind, plus vegan water-gyoza with a rice-flour wrapper (gluten-free available on request). The Tokyo Station Ichibangai and official listings note staff ask about wheat allergy and cook the GF order in a separate pot — a meaningful positive. HOWEVER this is a small 26-seat counter shop that simultaneously boils regular WHEAT ramen noodles, and the flagship 醤油らーめん is made with 生醤油 (wheat-based raw soy sauce); the standard broths/tsuyu and shared ladles/counter mean cross-contamination is possible. Choose the SHIO (salt) base, not shoyu. This is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen/fryer, so a strict celiac should confirm the separate-pot handling in person on the day and avoid any soy-sauce-based bowl.
tokyo3_y_28.vegan_detail: Several genuinely animal-free dishes: ヴィーガン担々麺 (vegan tantanmen — soy-milk/sesame broth with soy-meat crumbles and chili oil), a vegan veggie-soba (vegetable broth), ヴィーガン水餃子 (vegan water-gyoza, rice-flour wrapper), and a soy-milk soft-serve dessert. IMPORTANT caveats: the popular キノコベジソバ (mushroom veggie-soba) is only vegan when you ORDER IT WITHOUT the 鶏チャーシュー (chicken chashu) and mushroom oil — the default bowl is not vegan. The 貝塩らーめん (clam-salt ramen) is bonito- and shellfish-based — not vegan. Vegan items are served from roughly 10:00. Confirm no dashi/bonito when ordering, since the kitchen also runs animal broths.

chef_bio.background: Founder of the Soranoiro group. Worked at Kumurasaki in the Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum as a university student, then after a company job and a stint at Takechan Niboshi Ramen, joined Hakata Ippudo in March 2000 and trained across many departments for about 10 years 10 months (cooking, store operations, staff development). Opened the first Soranoiro in Kojimachi, Tokyo in June 2011. Now also works as a ramen consultant (frozen-noodle advisor, flour-company advisor, shop production and product development).
chef_bio.philosophy: Mission 'まだ見ぬお客様と業界の発展のために' (for customers yet unseen and the advancement of the industry). Carries the Ippudo principle '変わらないために変わり続けること' (to stay the same you must keep changing). Named the company from the Heart Sutra's 色即是空・空即是色. Sees himself as a chef, not just a ramen-shop operator, and deliberately gives each branch a different menu. Set out to make a ramen shop a woman could enter alone, and built vegetables into the noodles, broth and toppings.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegetable ramen (ベジソバ) — vegetables in the noodles, broth and toppings — plus vegan ramen and a gluten-free (brown-rice-noodle) ramen. The Soranoiro veggie/vegan soba was featured in the Michelin Guide Tokyo (Bib Gourmand, 2015–2017).

anecdotes.text: Trained about 10 years and 10 months at Hakata Ippudo (joined March 2000) before opening the first Soranoiro in Kojimachi in June 2011.
Developed the vegan ramen after a well-received appearance at Paris Ramen Week in 2014, building a vegetable-based broth enriched with carrot and red-pepper puree.

Over ~13 years has created around 300 seasonal limited ramen to connect diners with regional producers nationwide — including sustaining Sanriku seaweed purchases for 8 years to support post-tsunami recovery.

Currency check: the Gnavi page was last updated 17 August 2026 and lists rakugo dates through 24 October, so a published closure of 21–24 September 2026 for 設備改修 and lunch-only service on 5 September are both current, not stale. Search legs, all HTTP 200 and all read: Yahoo Japan for 「薮伊豆総本店 日本橋 そば」 and for 「薮伊豆総本店 野川 六代目 日本橋 落語」; the shop's own site (index, こだわり, お品書き, 店舗情報, 店内のご案内, お取り寄せ, 寄席); s.tabelog.com; r.gnavi.co.jp; nihonbashi-tokyo.jp; and the Shizuoka Prefecture PDF, which a server-side fetch could not parse and which was read by extracting the text locally. tokyo3_cafe_vava.gf_detail: The signature "VAVAパンケーキ" batter is made with 100% domestic rice flour and, per the official site and menu, uses NO wheat flour (「小麦粉を一切使わない」); it is sweetened with beet sugar (てん菜糖). There is also a gluten-free spaghetti (グルテンフリースパゲッティ, 国産米粉100%: 天使の海老 / アラビアータ). So real, deliberate GF items exist. BUT this is NOT a dedicated gluten-free kitchen: the same menu openly serves wheat-based dishes — モンティクリスト (French toast on bread), 天使の海老バーガー (wheat buns), 天然酵母パン・ド・カンパーニュ (bread), and スコーン. Wheat flour and bread are prepared in the same kitchen, so a strict celiac faces genuine cross-contamination risk (shared surfaces, flour dust, shared griddle/utensils); none of the sources confirm separate prep or a dedicated fryer. Published allergen labels on the GF pancakes note egg (卵), dairy (乳), soy (大豆), shrimp (えび) and yam (山芋). Verdict: the rice-flour pancake and the 米粉 spaghetti are legitimate GF orders, but confirm cross-contamination handling in person — the "gluten-free" branding refers to specific items, not a wheat-free premises.
tokyo3_cafe_vava.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly menu. It is a dessert/tea cafe: the rice-flour pancakes list egg (卵) and dairy (乳) as allergens, and the flagship drink is Ceylon royal milk tea (dairy). Cream, soft-serve (VAVAソフト) and cheese-forward savory items dominate. A VAVAサラダ / VAVAミニサラダ exists and might be adaptable, but no vegan items are advertised and hidden dairy/egg is pervasive. A vegan should ask item-by-item and not count on a full meal here.

chef_bio.philosophy: Balancing 「美味」と「健康」 (deliciousness and health): a gluten-free 100% domestic rice-flour pancake batter for a delicate melt-in-mouth texture, and body-friendly beet sugar (てん菜糖) from domestic sugar beets instead of cane sugar.

tokyo3_ginza.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. A tsukemen and chuka-soba counter: thick tsukemen noodles and flat wavy ramen noodles, wheat by default, with no gluten-free noodle in any source. The dipping soup is a seafood-and-pork-bone blend, and its seasoning is not published.

tokyo3_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · tsukemen] Owner Yaginuma Eiji worked in Japanese restaurants and ramen shops through his twenties. Hooked by the tsukemen boom in his thirties, he worked out this dipping soup on his own palate and opened in 2010, in what was then a dark Ginza back lane. The name, 'hazy moon', comes from the yellow light the shop cast there. The draw is the rich seafood-and-pork-bone tsukemen. Diners call it very rich but never heavy, with thick, springy noodles and torch-seared chashu, finished with a yuzu-scented soup to thin the dip. The clear niboshi chuka soba has been on the menu since opening day. In 2026 the shop sits in a new spot beside Ginza Kagari, with 8 counter seats.

chef_bio.background: Yaginuma loved cooking from a young age and worked in Japanese restaurants and ramen shops from his twenties, eating his way round other shops. In his thirties, during the tsukemen boom led by Ikebukuro Taishōken, he chose tsukemen over the izakaya he had been planning, and developed the soup alone (自分の舌だけで研究を重ね). He knew Ginza from his washoku years and took a suitable lot there in 2010.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「どことも違うスープを作り出したかった」 — to make a seafood-and-pork-bone soup unlike anyone else's, from the most familiar tsukemen ingredients.
chef_bio.specialty: Rich seafood–pork-bone tsukemen with thick, springy noodles and torch-seared chashu; clear niboshi chuka soba with flat wavy noodles.

anecdotes.text: 「お店を開いた2010年はこの辺は店もあまりなく、暗い路地のような場所でしたよ」 — he named the shop 朧月 for the yellow light it cast into that dark lane.
About seventy percent of customers order the rich or special tsukemen; the chuka soba has been served since opening and has its own regulars.

tokyo3_higash.notes: [Ramen · Shimbashi's Haru-chan, second shop] The Ginza branch, opened July 2024, of はるちゃんラーメン. The original is a 6-seat counter in Shimbashi that its owner, Haru-chan, opened in 2021 and runs single-handed. BAILA reports Bib Gourmand selections every year since 2023. The bowl is chuka soba in a salt soup of pork, niboshi and vegetable stock. It is filled to the brim so it stays hot, with flat Daruma Seimen noodles, chashu of two cuts sliced to order, and the shop's signature pastel fu. Regular and large cost the same. A chili topping comes in strengths 1–5. Limited bowls rotate (a curry chuka soba in October 2026). There are 10 counter seats, a ticket machine and a mostly overseas crowd.

tokyo3_ginza_47.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Rengatei is a yōshoku (Japanese-Western) house built on breaded, fried dishes. The pork cutlet uses fresh panko and is fried in a secret blend of three oils, and the menu also has fried prawns and other cutlets. The Meiji-style omurice is seasoned with a little sugar-and-soy, and Japanese soy sauce contains wheat by default. No gluten-free dish is mentioned.
tokyo3_ginza_47.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The consommé is a beef-tendon bouillon with vegetables, the omurice is egg with minced meat, and the signature dishes are pork, prawns and beef.
tokyo3_ginza_47.hours_raw: Mon–Sat & holidays 11:15–15:00 (L.O. 14:00) and 17:30–21:00 (L.O. 20:00); closed Sundays (Tabelog; "please contact us for changes on specific days"). Cash only.
tokyo3_ginza_47.notes: [Mom & Pop · yōshoku since 1895] A Ginza Western-food house founded in 1895 by Kida Motojirō, at a time when Western cooking was eaten only in hotels and at court. He wanted ordinary people to be able to order a single Western dish. His great-grandson, Kida Kōichirō, runs it today as the fourth-generation owner, with long-serving staff. The house credits itself with much of Japanese yōshoku as we know it. Its pork cutlet adapted the veal côtelette with pork, because veal was scarce. Shredded cabbage beside the cutlet, it says, started when cooks were drafted in the Russo-Japanese War and there was no one to make warm vegetables. Rice on a flat plate and two omurice, both from around 1900, are also on its list. The original omurice began as a staff meal, with egg and rice mixed together. There are four floors, including a tatami room, and bricks from the old Ginza brick district hang on the ground-floor wall. Cash only.

chef_bio.origin: Ginza; founded 1895 by his great-grandfather 木田元次郎 (Kida Motojirō)
chef_bio.background: Kida Motojirō opened Rengatei in 1895 so that ordinary people could order Western dishes one at a time instead of only as hotel or court courses. Four generations on, the house keeps its 'casual yōshoku-ya' spirit, with long-serving staff working alongside the fourth-generation owner.
chef_bio.philosophy: 気取らない「洋食屋」の精神 — the unpretentious spirit of a neighbourhood Western-food house.
chef_bio.specialty: Original pork cutlet; Meiji-born omurice and the original mixed-rice omurice; consommé jelly.

anecdotes.text: The pork cutlet: the founder's version of the French côtelette de veau, made with pork because veal was hard to get.
Shredded cabbage with the cutlet began during the Russo-Japanese War, when many cooks were conscripted and raw cabbage replaced cooked vegetables — the house says it stuck because it was refreshing.
Both omurice date from about 1900; the original — egg and rice mixed — began as a staff meal for practising omelettes.
Most of the popular dishes were once staff meals (まかない), the original omurice among them.
The cutlet fat is a secret blend of three oils.

tokyo3_ginza_54.notes: [Tonkatsu · since 1927] Ginza's first tonkatsu specialist. It opened in 1927 under founder Shibuya Nobukatsu, a former pharmacist who drew on that training to create a thick, sweet tonkatsu sauce from apple and onion, which the house calls the original chūnō sauce. He also cut fillet into bite-size pieces ('hitokuchi katsu'), put katsu between slices of bread, and created the 'special katsudon', a loin cutlet bound in egg with a second, unbroken egg on top. The family business, 有限会社梅林 under president Shibuya Masaya, is in its third generation. It has franchise counters at Haneda Airport, in Waikiki and in Seoul. The head shop is in the basement of its own building. It uses Kagoshima black pork, Yamagata Tsuyahime rice (free refills) and seasonal cabbage, and the fillet-katsu sandwich is packed in old-style wood-shaving boxes.

tokyo3_ginza_57.notes: [Mom & Pop · Japanese omakase, Michelin ★★] Owner-chef Takemasa Shinohara trained at Kyoto restaurants including Sangencha and opened his own Shinohara in his hometown of Kōnan, Shiga, in his twenties. When it had become a destination, he left it behind and started again in Ginza in October 2016. A small lantern leads down to a calm room around an L-shaped counter of white wood, thirteen seats, with tableware down to old Baccarat. One omakase course (¥35,000 including tax in 2026, with seasonal extras such as crab or charcoal-grilled beef rice), changing monthly. Its signature is the hassun, a lavish platter of the season themed to the calendar, such as the Double Ninth in September. Michelin two stars, and The Tabelog Award Gold every year from 2017 to 2026. In October 2026 it marked ten years in Ginza and twenty since the first Shinohara, and many of his former cooks now run fully booked restaurants of their own. Book months ahead.

tokyo3__70.gf_detail: No GF information could be verified for this specific shop — nothing was published online, so treat everything below as unconfirmed and ask in person. As a general matter, an ordinary Japanese soba-dokoro is HIGH RISK for celiacs: (1) most "soba" here is nihachi (二八) — roughly 20% wheat flour blended into the buckwheat, so the noodles themselves usually contain wheat unless a dish is explicitly labeled juwari/十割; (2) even juwari soba is NOT safe — the tsuyu/mentsuyu dipping and soup base is made with regular wheat-based soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu), and any tempura is wheat-batter fried in shared oil; (3) buckwheat and wheat flour are milled/dusted in the same kitchen, so cross-contamination on boards, boiling water and utensils is expected. No dedicated GF kitchen or fryer is known. A celiac should not assume any dish here is safe without a direct, careful conversation (ideally with a Japanese allergy card), and realistically should treat this shop as unsuitable unless staff can specifically confirm juwari noodles AND a gluten-free tamari-based tsuyu — which was NOT documented.
tokyo3__70.vegan_detail: The listing signals "vegetarian options," but nothing vegan-specific could be verified for this shop. The critical hidden-animal risk at any soba shop is the broth: soba tsuyu, kake-soba soup and mentsuyu are almost always built on katsuo-dashi (bonito/skipjack) and often niboshi (dried sardine), so even a plain zaru/mori soba dipping sauce or a "vegetable" tempura soba is typically non-vegan. Tempura may also share oil with shrimp/fish. A vegan should ask specifically whether a kombu-only (kelp) dashi is available and whether any dish can be served without bonito — this was not confirmed. Do not assume plant-based unless staff verify the dashi.

No dedicated GF kitchen or fryer. Only okayu (plain rice porridge) and fresh fruit are inherently low-risk, but they arrive as part of a mixed set. tokyo3__104.vegan_detail: Not a vegan/vegetarian restaurant despite the temple setting and "shojin-inspired" marketing. The signature 18-dish breakfast explicitly contains fish and meat: ikura (salmon roe) with yuba, nori-mentaiko (cod roe), octopus in shio-koji, Tsukiji Kimbun fish tofu, aigamo (duck) with sansho, plus tamagoyaki (egg). The miso soup uses standard dashi (bonito likely — hidden animal stock). No dedicated vegan menu is published. Some individual plant components exist (black beans, kombu tsukudani, soy-braised eggplant, tofu, pickles, fruit, matcha jelly), and PRONTO café drinks/sweets are available, but a fully vegan plate is not offered as such — a vegan must confirm each item and avoid the set breakfast. Flag hidden dashi/bonito in the soup and any simmered vegetable dishes.

chef_bio.background: The café is operated by PRONTO Corporation (a nationwide Japanese coffee/café chain) as an official concession inside the Tsukiji Hongwanji Information Center, opened when the center was completed in 2017. There is no single celebrity chef; the concept is a temple-grounds Japanese café. The signature 18-dish breakfast is assembled from small dishes sourced from long-established shops in the Tsukiji Outer Market rather than cooked by a named head chef.
chef_bio.philosophy: A 'temple café' concept: an accessible, tourist-friendly Japanese breakfast whose 18-small-bowl format is a nod to Buddhist/shojin aesthetics and the number of Amida Buddha's vows, presented as a calm start to the day overlooking the main hall — marketed as shojin-motif rather than strict shojin ryori.
chef_bio.specialty: 18品の朝ごはん (18-dish breakfast): 16 small side dishes plus okayu (rice porridge), miso soup and tea.

anecdotes.text: The 18-dish breakfast's small side dishes are drawn from renowned shops of the Tsukiji Outer Market (e.g., fish tofu by Tsukiji Kimbun), tying the café to the surrounding market rather than an in-house kitchen.
The breakfast is made in limited daily quantities and frequently sells out before the 10:30 end of breakfast service, so the café offers online reservations for the morning slot.

tokyo3__113.notes: [Mom & Pop · tempura master] Kondō Fumio, born in 1947, joined the tempura kitchen of the Yama-no-ue Hotel in Ochanomizu after high school and became its head chef at 23. He opened his own counter in Ginza in 1991 and, more than 50 years into his career, still fries at the counter himself at lunch and dinner. His batter is cut as thin as possible so it doesn't soak up oil, and he treats tempura as a steamed dish too, timing the carry-over heat inside the batter. Above all he brought vegetables into high-end Edo-mae tempura, which had been seafood-only. His signature is a stump-thick sweet potato fried slowly for about 30 minutes. It has held two Michelin stars since 2008. He was named a 現代の名工 (Contemporary Master Craftsman) in 2019, and in 2023 became the first tempura chef to receive Michelin's Mentor Chef Award. Two counters of 12 and 8 seats, by reservation.

chef_bio.philosophy: 「天ぷらは、料理人がゲストをお招きする料理」 — tempura is the cook inviting the guest; and 「天ぷらの本質は蒸し料理」, tempura is at heart a steamed dish.

anecdotes.text: Vegetables were once beneath fine tempura — 「元々、天ぷらの世界で、野菜は邪道だったんですよ」 — and he set out to change that so tempura could stand beside sushi as Japan's representative cuisine.
The sweet potato, thick as a tree stump and more than 10 cm across, fries for about 30 minutes to seal in its moisture and sweetness — his aim was to beat a roasted sweet potato.
He tastes vegetables on the farm before contracting them, and asks growers to thin a pumpkin vine from five fruits to three so each is better.
The shredded-carrot tempura, fried all at once, is his original.
2019 「現代の名工」 (government award for master craftsmen); 2023 Michelin Mentor Chef Award, the first tempura chef to receive it; Michelin two stars every year since 2008.

tokyo3__123.gf_detail: Not safe for a celiac. 更科そば (sarashina) noodles are milled from the refined white inner endosperm core of the buckwheat groat (更科粉／一番粉, confirmed on JA Wikipedia). That pure starch binds poorly, so sarashina soba is bound with a HIGH proportion of wheat flour (小麦粉) as tsunagi — typically MORE wheat than ordinary 二八 soba — meaning the noodles themselves contain significant gluten. There is no juwari/GF noodle here, and even juwari would be 'ask' at best. The dipping tsuyu/broth is made with standard wheat-fermented soy sauce (醤油). The visible menu (Tabelog) is wheat-heavy throughout: tempura soba (天ぷら — wheat batter), curry seiro / curry soba (curry roux normally contains wheat flour), tanuki soba (tenkasu = fried wheat), and katsudon sets (panko-breaded pork). No dedicated GF kitchen, no dedicated fryer, and no allergen program was found. A celiac should not eat here.
tokyo3__123.vegan_detail: Hidden fish is pervasive. The cold mori/zaru soba noodles are flour-and-water (no egg), but the standard tsuyu is a bonito/katsuobushi (fish) dashi and hot broths (kake soba) use bonito–kombu dashi, so nearly every served dish carries fish stock. Tempura and tanuki (tenkasu) items share frying oil with animal-based fries. No vegan menu, no vegan dashi, and no plant-based labeling were found. At most a strict vegan could eat plain cold soba noodles while declining the tsuyu and bringing/confirming a fish-free dipping sauce — and would still need to verify the noodles themselves and any garnish. Confirm every broth/sauce is dashi-free before ordering.

tokyo3__144.gf_detail: The restaurant explicitly brands its signature curries as "小麦粉を使わないグルテンフリーカリー" (gluten-free curry made WITHOUT wheat flour) on its official site. chef_bio.background: Founder and CEO of YUWAERU Inc. (株式会社結わえる), which he started in 2009 and whose Kuramae flagship (蔵前本店) opened as the company's home base. Before founding the company he worked at a major consulting firm on healthcare-related corporate consulting, where he grew convinced that lifestyle diseases were rising because of drastic changes in modern eating and living, and set out to build 'a world where people fundamentally don't get sick.' He styles himself the '玄米社長' (Brown Rice President) and a food & wellness researcher.
chef_bio.philosophy: The company name 結わえる means to 'tie/knot together' — bridging traditional Japanese living culture with modern life for a sustainable 21st-century lifestyle. His signature idea, 一日一膳 玄米生活 ('one bowl of brown rice a day'), centers on his 寝かせ玄米® (aged/fermented brown rice) as a complete staple food. He preaches achievable, non-perfectionist wellness — 'health at 70 points is fine' — rather than restrictive dieting, and links personal health to the health of the planet: choosing what you eat is choosing what future you want to live in.

tokyo3_gugga.gf_detail: Important: "GUGGA" the brand is wheat-flour-free (its cookies/brownies use organic oat flour, no wheat), BUT this entry is the vegan SOUP BREAKFAST served inside CLANN BY THE RIVER, an omnivore riverside café at LYURO Tokyo Kiyosumi 2F — there is no dedicated GF kitchen or fryer. Sides are bread or rice (pick rice if avoiding egg/dairy in bread). This is NOT an all-vegan restaurant; it is an omnivore hotel café with a dependable vegan soup and GUGGA vegan baked goods.

chef_bio.chef_name: 山後静音 (Shizune Yamago) — founder of GUGGA (brand that produces the vegan soup); the on-site cook at CLANN BY THE RIVER is not documented
chef_bio.background: GUGGA was founded in 2018 in Kamakura, Kanagawa. Shizune discovered veganism while studying at university in Hawaii, where her roommates were vegan, which reshaped how she saw plant-based food. tokyo3__159.gf_detail: Not safe to rely on for celiac. The house specialty is 生麩 (nama-fu / raw wheat gluten), sourced from Kyoto's 半兵衛麩 — it is essentially pure wheat and appears throughout the signature dishes (生麩田楽, 生麩と季節野菜の揚げ出し, and the flagship 湯葉クリームコロッケ which packs yuba AND nama-fu into a flour-breaded, deep-fried croquette). Menu leans heavily on deep-fried items (揚げ湯葉サラダ, croquette, agedashi) with no indication of a dedicated fryer, so shared-oil and flour/panko cross-contamination is likely. Standard Japanese soy sauce and tsuyu (wheat-containing) and dashi season most dishes. A few items are naturally wheat-free in isolation (自家製豆腐, 湯葉 sashimi, vegetable obanzai) but there is no GF program, labeling, or allergen handling — a celiac should treat this as a wheat-forward kitchen. Note: any juwari/soba is not offered as a GF claim here regardless.
tokyo3__159.vegan_detail: Plant-forward but NOT a vegan/精進 restaurant — it is an omnivore washoku house that also serves wagyu (天草黒毛和牛). She was diagnosed with celiac disease roughly four years ago and, after struggling to find safe food at restaurants, convenience stores and supermarkets across Japan, opened Oh Nana! in March 2026 — she frames it as Japan's first Western-standard, fully celiac-safe restaurant. The venue took over the site of the former organic restaurant ROSY near Kanda Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: Create an inclusive space where everyone — gluten-free or not — can share good Japanese food together and make happy memories, so that people with dietary restrictions no longer have to eat apart from family and friends. tokyo3__161.gf_detail: Genuinely strong GF setup for a Tokyo izakaya — but read the caveats. The house soy sauce is a gluten-free broad-bean (空豆) tamari-style shoyu, salt is Okinawan Nuchima-su, and cooking is advertised as roughly 98% non-oil on the teppan. The omakase vegetable course is described by the restaurant/Vegewel as 完全グルテンフリー (completely gluten-free), and the shop explicitly advertises accommodating グルテンフリー / ビーガン / 五葷抜き requests. It is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen: wheat lives on the premises — a Turkish simit/シミット sesame bread and a hummus set, plus an attached bakery whose ~30 breads are mostly wheat. Okonomiyaki uses 玄米・大和芋・米粉 (brown rice, yam, rice flour) as binder rather than wheat flour, but is cooked on the same teppan as bread items. A celiac should order the explicitly GF course, confirm the GF broad-bean soy sauce is used on their specific dishes, and flag cross-contact from bread/flour and the shared teppan. (No juwari-soba concern here — this is not a soba shop.)
tokyo3__161.vegan_detail: Plant-based vegetable izakaya (野菜居酒屋) with a dedicated vegan course (~¥3,500 pre-tax) and vegan-cheese (ビーガンチーズ) dishes — avocado/vegan-cheese spring rolls, vegan-cheese-baked gourd with oyster mushroom, strawberry & baby-greens okonomiyaki, hot teppan potato salad. Listed on Vegewel and Veganmania as a vegan destination, and 五葷抜き (no onion/garlic) is available on request. Dashi appears plant-based (no bonito/dashi-fish mentioned anywhere) but not explicitly confirmed — worth a check. The concept is framed as letting vegans and meat-lovers dine together comfortably (ビーガンの方と肉好きの方が), so confirm any individual dish is fully animal-free; the attached bakery also includes non-vegan breads (only ~1/3 of its breads are vegan).

chef_bio.philosophy: Build an inclusive table where people with different dietary needs — vegan, gluten-free, five-pungent-free, and meat-lovers — can eat together without anyone feeling singled out, in a retro-modern space, using vegetables as the star and gluten-free broad-bean soy sauce plus near-oil-free cooking as the default.

tokyo3_t_s.gf_detail: Not safe for a celiac. T'sたんたん is a vegan RAMEN counter and its core noodle is standard wheat 中華麺 (Chinese-style wheat noodle) — gluten by definition. The tantan/soy tare is built on ordinary Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, and the sesame-tantan base is a shared wheat-exposed kitchen. No dedicated gluten-free noodle, dedicated fryer, or gluten protocol was found for THIS Gransta Tokyo station location. Note: the brand's sister shop "T's Kitchen" (Ueno) and the flagship T's Restaurant in Jiyugaoka do advertise gluten-free noodle swaps / GF dishes, but that is a different address — do not assume the station stand offers it. A celiac should treat this location as wheat-based and, if they want to try the brand, go to the GF-equipped sister location instead.
tokyo3_t_s.vegan_detail: [Held at "some vegan options" 2026-08-20] The "fully vegan" label was contradicted by this record's own cited sources. Fully plant-based — this is one of Tokyo's landmark vegan ramen shops. The entire menu uses no meat, seafood, dairy, or eggs ("肉・魚介・乳製品・卵を一切使わずに"), and the broth is a vegetable/kombu-style umami base rather than bonito/animal dashi, so there is no hidden fish-stock trap that plagues most Japanese ramen. Because the whole kitchen is vegan, there is essentially no animal cross-contact risk. An "oriental veg" (no onion/garlic, allium-free) option is also available. Confirm nothing is topped with honey-style condiments if you are strict, but the shop is designed and marketed as 100% vegan.

chef_bio.background: Founder and representative of T's Restaurant. Born March 1956, a Keio University graduate. She was originally a lover of animal foods (fatty tuna toro, cream dishes) and turned to plant-based eating after a close friend fell ill and was advised by doctors to cut animal products, which crystallized her belief in preventative health through everyday food. She opened the flagship T's Restaurant in Jiyugaoka in September 2009 and created the T'sたんたん vegan-ramen spin-off, which now runs multiple locations across Tokyo train stations and Narita Airport. She is a director of the Japan Plant-Based Market Association.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'Smile Veg' (スマイルベジ) — communicate the importance of health through food that is delicious enough that anyone, vegan or not, is happy to eat it. Vegan food should be an accessible, joyful default (in schools, offices, airlines, stations), not a compromise.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan tantanmen and plant-based ramen with animal-free umami depth (no meat, fish, egg, dairy, or bonito dashi).

anecdotes.text: A former marbled-toro-and-cream lover, Shimokawa switched to plant-based cooking after a close friend became ill and doctors advised reducing animal products; she began serving her family tofu-based 'meat sauce' pasta and noticed her own mornings became lighter and more energetic.

T's Restaurant was born in a near-magical 5-day span in May 2009: a chance meeting with a photographer led to a plate designer who imagined a 'mountain-lodge-style' natural restaurant; the next day she spotted a newly built space near Jiyugaoka Station, called on impulse, and one unit was free. It opened on the 25th — a date she says kept recurring at every milestone.

Her vegan noodles were adopted as international-airline in-flight meals, and she published what is described as Japan's first home-use vegan recipe book, 『奇跡のごちそう』 (2013); her Smile Veg work has extended to corporate cafeterias and school lunches for tens of thousands of students in Tsukuba.

tokyo3_lei.gf_detail: This is a genuinely wheat-free establishment, not a place that merely offers a few GF items. The restaurant's own name and concept is 「小麦を使わない国産ビストロ」— "a domestic bistro that does not use wheat." A gluten-free blogger who visited reports the chef himself has a wheat allergy ("シェフが小麦アレルギーとのことで相談もできて安心"), so no wheat flour is used anywhere: bread and quiche/pastry are made with rice flour (米粉), and even the signature spice curry is 小麦粉不使用 (no wheat-flour roux), thickened instead with house bouillon and long-cooked whole onions. Because there is no wheat in the kitchen, the usual Japanese cross-contamination traps (tempura batter, shared fryer with breaded items, flour dusting) do not apply here. The one thing NOT independently confirmed on any source page is the soy sauce / seasoning base: ordinary Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and while a fully wheat-free bistro almost certainly uses a wheat-free tamari, a celiac should still confirm the soy sauce and any sauce/curry base directly on-site. Overall this is one of the safest-looking GF options in the Akihabara area for a celiac, precisely because the whole kitchen is built around avoiding wheat.
tokyo3_lei.vegan_detail: Vegan is not the focus — the menu centers on domestic meat and animal products: Miyagi (Oshika Peninsula) venison cooked sous-vide with beet sauce, mochi-pork ("もち豚") smoked/curry dishes, spinach quiche and chocolate terrine (egg/dairy), and a house bouillon that is very likely animal-based. There are plant-forward items (grilled seasonal vegetables, rice-flour bread), so a vegetarian or flexible diner can eat, but a strict vegan must confirm the dashi/bouillon and ask for meat- and dairy-free versions. No explicitly labelled vegan set was found. Note the GF strength here does NOT extend to vegan — treat those as separate questions on-site.
